partA.script:
Agent: Good afternoon, WorkSpace Solutions, how can I help you today?

Caller: Hi, I'm calling to enquire about renting a desk at one of your co-working spaces. I've been working from home but I need somewhere quieter a few days a week.

Agent: Sure, I can help with that. We have three locations — Riverside, Central, and Northgate. Which area suits you best?

Caller: Probably Central, since it's close to where I live.

Agent: Great. Our Central branch offers a hot-desk membership for eighty-five pounds a month, which gives you access three days a week, or a full membership for one hundred and forty pounds for unlimited access.

Caller: I think three days a week would be enough for now. What are the opening hours?

Agent: The Central branch is open from seven in the morning until nine at night, Monday to Friday, and from nine until five on Saturdays.

Caller: Perfect. And is there parking available?

Agent: There's a car park next door, but members get a discounted rate of four pounds for the whole day instead of the usual eight.

Caller: That's good to know. How do I sign up?

Agent: I can email you the registration form right now — could I take your email address?

partB.script:
Host: This week on Working Lives, we're discussing remote work with two guests — Marcus Webb, an HR director, and Sofia Alves, who has worked remotely for six years. Marcus, what's the biggest challenge you see employers facing?

Marcus: Honestly, it's measuring productivity fairly. Some managers still equate visible activity with actual output, which creates unnecessary pressure on remote staff to appear busy rather than focus on results.

Sofia: I'd agree with that, but from an employee's side, my biggest challenge has actually been isolation. I miss the casual conversations you have in an office that often lead to good ideas.

Host: Do you think companies should mandate a certain number of in-office days?

Marcus: We've settled on two days a week as a minimum, and honestly it's worked well for us — it preserves some collaboration time without erasing the flexibility employees value.

Sofia: I'm more sceptical of mandates in general. I think it should depend on the role and the individual, rather than a fixed company-wide rule.

Host: And looking ahead, where do you both see this heading in the next five years?

Marcus: I expect most large companies will settle into some kind of hybrid model as the default, rather than fully remote or fully in-office.

Sofia: I actually think fully remote will become more common for specialised roles, as companies compete for talent regardless of location.

reading.title: The Hybrid Work Debate: Where Is the Middle Ground?
reading.article:
When large numbers of office workers began working from home in the early 2020s, many assumed the shift was temporary. Several years on, however, hybrid and remote arrangements have become a permanent feature of many industries, and organisations are still experimenting to find a model that satisfies both business needs and employee expectations.

Proponents of remote work point to substantial gains in employee satisfaction and, in many cases, measurable productivity. Removing a daily commute frees up time that employees can redirect toward rest, family, or focused work, and surveys consistently show that flexibility ranks among the top factors candidates consider when evaluating job offers. Companies that offer remote options often report a wider pool of applicants, since location is no longer a limiting factor.

However, executives in favour of returning to the office argue that spontaneous, informal interaction — the kind that happens at a shared coffee machine or in a chance corridor conversation — is difficult to replicate virtually, and that this kind of interaction disproportionately benefits younger or newer employees who are still building professional networks and learning organisational norms. Some studies have also suggested that fully remote teams take slightly longer to resolve ambiguous problems that require rapid, informal back-and-forth discussion.

Hybrid models, which combine a set number of in-office days with remote flexibility, have emerged as the most common compromise. Yet even here, disagreement persists over the details: should the specific in-office days be fixed company-wide to maximise overlap, or left to individual teams to coordinate? Fixed schedules tend to guarantee more colleagues are present simultaneously, but they can feel inflexible to employees managing childcare or long commutes, whereas team-level flexibility increases employee satisfaction but risks near-empty offices on some days and overcrowded ones on others.

What is increasingly clear is that a single nationwide or even industry-wide policy is unlikely to suit every organisation. Factors such as the nature of the work, the age and experience of the workforce, and the cost of office space all shape which arrangement makes the most sense for a given company.

task1.prompt:
You recently started a new job that requires you to work from home two days a week, but you do not have suitable equipment. Write a letter to your manager.

In your letter:
- explain your situation
- describe what equipment you need
- suggest how the company could help
task1.outline:
Para 1: State purpose of the letter and new working arrangement.
Para 2: Explain the specific problem (e.g. no proper desk/monitor).
Para 3: List equipment needed and suggest a practical solution (reimbursement, company-supplied equipment).
Para 4: Polite closing, request a response.

task2.prompt: In many countries, more people are choosing to work from home rather than in a traditional office. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
task2.outline:
Intro: paraphrase + thesis (advantages outweigh / disadvantages outweigh / balanced).
Body 1: Advantages — flexibility, reduced commute, wider talent pool.
Body 2: Disadvantages — isolation, collaboration difficulty, blurred work-life boundaries.
Conclusion: restate position with brief justification.

feedback.before:
Working from home have many advantage for worker. First, they don't need to spend time for travel to office, so they can use this time for sleep more or spend time with family. Second, worker can focus better because office is very noisy sometimes and many people disturb them.

But working from home also have some problem. Worker can feel lonely because they don't meet colleague every day. Also, some worker can't stop working because their house and office is same place, so they work too much time.
feedback.comment:
문법: 'have many advantage' → 'has many advantages'; 'time for sleep more' → 'more time to sleep'; 'also have some problem' → 'also has some problems' 로 수정.

연결어: 문단 간 전환이 First/Second/But 정도로 단순함. 'On the other hand', 'However' 같은 격식 있는 연결어 사용 권장.

내용 전개: 각 장점/단점이 한 문장으로 짧게 끝나 근거(예시, 결과)가 부족함. 구체적인 예시를 한두 개 추가하면 밴드 상승에 도움됨.

어휘: 'problem' 대신 'drawback', 'downside' 등 다양한 어휘 사용 권장.
feedback.after:
Working from home offers several notable advantages for employees. Firstly, eliminating the daily commute frees up a significant amount of time, which workers can redirect toward rest or spending quality time with family. Secondly, many employees report being able to concentrate more effectively at home, since a typical office environment often involves frequent interruptions from colleagues or background noise.

However, this arrangement is not without its drawbacks. Many remote workers report a growing sense of isolation, having lost the daily face-to-face contact with colleagues that once provided both social support and opportunities for informal collaboration. Furthermore, because the boundary between home and workplace becomes blurred, some employees find it difficult to switch off at the end of the day, which can ultimately lead to overwork and burnout.
